name: Height-increasing supplements
lead: Height-increasing supplements are over-the-counter products, typically vitamin, mineral, amino-acid or herbal blends, marketed to people who want to be taller, either by supporting growth in teenagers or by helping others reach their genetic height potential. Height changes how a person looks and is perceived, and these products are the pill-based option among height methods that also include stretching, posture work, shoe lifts and, in medicine, growth hormone.[1]

Reference sources describe height as strongly heritable (60 to 80 percent in twin studies) and as shaped by childhood nutrition and health, with chronic malnutrition able to slow growth and reduce adult height.[2] The nutrients typically included in these formulas, such as zinc, calcium, protein and vitamin D, are ones nutrition research links to growth in childhood. A systematic review of 63 zinc supplementation trials in children under five in low- and middle-income countries found no effect on height-for-age at the end of supplementation.[4]

The medical treatment for short stature is prescription growth hormone given under specialist care, and randomized trials report adult height gains of a few centimetres in selected children.[3][5][6] No published trial of a marketed height supplement in healthy people was located.
infobox: Zinc, calcium, vitamin D, amino acids, herbal extracts

paras: Products sold under this heading are generally multi-ingredient formulas. A looksmax.org thread on the subject quotes material from a height-advice website describing growth supplements and guides alongside stretching content, and one replier in the thread describes the supplements as vitamins that target what supports growth without addressing a root cause, and as costly with results that take a long time to show.[1]

Wikipedia reports that genetics accounts for most variation in height within a population, and that nutrition, protein intake and overall health shape growth in childhood and adolescence.[2] It states that females generally stop growing at about 15 to 16 and males at about 18 to 19.[2] Because supplements are marketed to both teenagers and adults, how much any product could matter depends on remaining growth potential, which the sources do not quantify for supplements.

Nutrition studies in children have looked at individual nutrients that appear in supplement blends. A systematic review of 63 trials with 27,372 children under five in low- and middle-income countries found zinc supplementation made no difference to height-for-age score at the end of supplementation [4]; an earlier meta-analysis in the same age group examined absolute length gains [7].

Wikipedia's article on idiopathic short stature describes growth hormone as the main medical treatment, estimates that it may move a child from about the 1st to the 10th percentile at a cost that can reach $100,000 or more, and records ethical and economic debate about its use.[3] The article does not discuss over-the-counter height supplements.[3]

Randomized trials of growth hormone in idiopathic short stature report adult height gains. One placebo-controlled trial in 68 peripubertal children found treated children ended about 3.7 cm taller than placebo [5], and a systematic review of three randomized trials covering 115 children reported adult heights 0.65 standard deviation scores above controls [6].

No trials of marketed height supplement products in healthy adolescents or adults were found. Related research includes trials of single nutrients in young children in low- and middle-income countries, such as zinc, which a 2019 systematic review of 63 trials found made no difference to height-for-age at the end of supplementation [4], and a 2011 meta-analysis of preventive zinc and linear growth [7]. These studies were in children at risk of undernutrition and are not tests of commercial height blends.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, height supplements appear in threads asking whether growth pills help teens or adults, often alongside discussion of stretching and other height methods.[1]

claims.claim: Growth supplements can help people grow taller or reach full potential.
claims.believers: Marketers and some forum posters describe vitamin-type formulas as supporting the nutrients growth requires; at least one poster says he has considered them.[1]
claims.experts: Reference sources attribute variation in height mainly to genetics and childhood nutrition [2], and a systematic review of zinc trials in young children found no effect on height-for-age [4]. No published trial has tested a marketed height supplement.

claims.claim: Supplements are too expensive and slow to be worth it.
claims.believers: A forum replier says they are costly, take a long time to show results and are just vitamins that do not tackle the root cause.[1]
claims.experts: No price or outcome studies of such products were located.

card.summary: OTC pills sold to make you taller; height is mostly genetic and no trial backs them for adults.
card.note: No published trials of marketed height supplements were found.

quick.overview:
Height supplements are over-the-counter blends marketed to help people grow taller. Forum users ask whether they help teens or adults, and some call them costly and slow.

Reference sources describe height as mostly genetic and shaped by childhood nutrition. No trial of a marketed height supplement was found.
quick.mechanism: Marketers say the vitamins and minerals support the nutrients growth needs. Sources describe nutrition as affecting growth in childhood, but none tests these products.
quick.risks: No safety data specific to height supplements were located. Prescription growth hormone is a separate, medically supervised treatment.

chain: Vitamin, mineral or herbal blend taken daily
Intended to supply nutrients growth depends on
angle.text: Users, mostly teenagers and young adults, take these blends hoping to support growth and reach full genetic height. Height is visible in how tall a person appears, which is why the products are marketed to those still growing.
